q.t: Lemon juice tastes sour. What kind of substance is it?
q.e: Sourness is the tongue's way of detecting acids. Lemon contains citric acid, so lemon juice is acidic.

q.t: What does an acid do to blue litmus paper?
q.e: Acid turns blue litmus red. That colour change is how litmus tells you an acid is present without tasting it.

q.t: What does a base do to red litmus paper?
q.e: A base turns red litmus blue — the opposite of what an acid does to blue litmus.

q.t: Sugar solution changes neither red nor blue litmus. So it is…
q.e: A neutral substance is neither acidic nor basic, so it has nothing to change either litmus colour.

q.t: Litmus is obtained from…
q.e: Litmus comes from lichens — a fungus and an alga living together.

q.t: Which acid is found in curd?
q.e: Curd is made when bacteria turn milk sugar into lactic acid; that is why curd is sour.

q.t: Which of these is basic?
q.e: Soap feels slippery and turns red litmus blue — signs of a base. The other three are sour, so they are acidic.

q.t: Acid + Base → ?
q.e: In neutralisation the acid and base cancel each other, forming a salt and water, and giving out some heat.

q.t: Which acid is in vinegar?
q.e: Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid.

q.t: A substance that shows different colours in acids and bases is called…
q.e: An acid–base indicator changes colour depending on the nature of the substance, so its colour tells you whether something is acidic or basic.

q.t: Turmeric paper turns red when dipped in…
q.e: Turmeric turns red only with bases. Soap is a base; the others are acidic or neutral, so turmeric stays yellow.

q.t: Why can't turmeric tell an acidic solution from a neutral one?
q.e: Turmeric only reacts to bases. With an acid and with a neutral it stays yellow, so the two look the same.

q.t: Red rose extract turns green in a solution. The solution is…
q.e: Rose extract goes red-ish in acids and green in bases, so green means basic.

q.t: An ant bite stings because the ant injects…
q.e: Ants inject formic acid. Knowing it is an acid tells you the remedy: something basic.

q.t: What should you rub on an ant bite?
q.e: Baking soda is a base; it neutralises the formic acid. Lemon juice or vinegar would add more acid.

q.t: A farmer's soil has become too acidic. What should be added?
q.e: Too much of one nature is fixed by adding the opposite. Lime is basic, so it neutralises the acid in the soil.

q.t: Amla is rich in which acid (also called Vitamin C)?
q.e: Ascorbic acid is Vitamin C, and amla is one of its richest sources.

q.t: When lemon juice and baking soda solution are mixed, the mixture becomes slightly warm. Why?
q.e: Acid + base → salt + water + heat. The heat released by neutralisation warms the mixture.

q.t: Which pair are both acidic?
q.e: Tamarind (tartaric acid) and vinegar (acetic acid) are both sour and acidic. Each other pair has a base or a neutral in it.

q.t: A curry stain on a white shirt turns red when washed with soap. This happens because…
o: Soap is a base and turmeric turns red with bases
q.e: Curry has turmeric, a natural indicator. Soap is basic, and turmeric turns red in a base.

q.t: A liquid turns blue litmus red and has no effect on red litmus. It is…
q.e: Blue → red is the sign of an acid. An acid has no reason to change red litmus, which is already the acid colour.

q.t: Solution X turns red litmus blue and turmeric red. X could be…
q.e: Both tests point to a base. Lime water is basic; the rest are acidic or neutral.

q.t: You have only turmeric paper and three bottles: acid, base, neutral. How many can you identify for sure?
q.e: Turmeric turns red only in the base. Acid and neutral both leave it yellow, so you can pick out the base but not tell the other two apart.

q.t: Lime water is added drop by drop to lemon juice that holds a strip of red litmus. When does the strip turn blue?
o: Once more base than acid has been added
q.e: First the base is used up cancelling the acid. Only once the acid is fully neutralised and extra base is present does the mixture become basic and turn red litmus blue.

q.t: Why must acidic factory waste be treated before it goes into a lake?
o: It harms fish and water life
It makes the water too cold
q.e: Acidic water damages living things in the lake. Adding a base neutralises the waste first.

q.t: Soil is too basic. Which helps?
q.e: Organic matter releases acids as it decays, which neutralise the extra base. Lime and baking soda would make the soil even more basic.

q.t: Hydrangea flowers are blue in one garden and pink in another. The blue garden's soil is…
q.e: Hydrangeas act like an indicator: acidic soil gives blue flowers, basic soil gives pink.

q.t: A cloth with onion smell is dipped in baking soda solution and the smell disappears. Onion here is acting as…
q.e: Olfactory means smell. The onion signals a base by losing its smell instead of changing colour.

q.t: Bitter gourd (karela) is bitter. Is it basic?
o: No — bitterness alone doesn't prove it
Yes — all bitter things are bases
Yes — it turns blue litmus red
No — it is acidic because it is green
q.e: Bitter taste is not a safe test. Karela is bitter but not basic. Only an indicator gives a reliable answer.

q.t: Which word best describes the result of mixing exactly enough acid with base?
q.e: When acid and base cancel each other completely, the process is neutralisation and the result is neither acidic nor basic.

q.t: Invisible ink: a message written with soap solution appears when sprayed with turmeric solution. What colour does it appear?
q.e: The soap left on paper is basic; turmeric turns red where it meets a base, so the letters show up red.

q.t: If the message were written with lemon juice and sprayed with turmeric, what would happen?
q.e: Lemon juice is acidic; turmeric doesn't change in acids, so the letters stay invisible.

q.t: Three unlabelled bottles: P turns blue litmus red; Q turns red litmus blue; R changes neither. Mixing P and Q in the right amounts gives a liquid that behaves like…
q.e: P is acidic, Q basic, R neutral. Enough acid plus base neutralise each other, so the mixture becomes neutral, like R.

q.t: Rose extract is red in solution S. Adding solution T slowly turns it green. Which is true?
o: S is acidic and T is basic
S is basic and T is acidic
S is neutral and T acidic
q.e: Red in rose extract means acid. Turning green means the mixture has become basic, so T must be a base that first neutralised S, then went past it.

q.t: A bee sting injects an acid. Which household item is the best first remedy?
q.e: To neutralise an acid you need a base. Baking soda is the only base in the list.

q.t: Why do we use indicators instead of tasting or touching to test a substance?
q.e: Some acids and bases burn skin or poison. Indicators show the nature by colour or smell, safely.

q.t: You only have blue litmus paper. Bottle A turns it red, B and C don't. What can you conclude?
o: A is acidic; B and C are basic or neutral
q.e: Blue litmus only reacts to acids. B and C could be basic or neutral — you'd need red litmus to split them.

q.t: Which test would separate the basic bottle from the neutral bottle in the last question?
q.e: A base turns red litmus blue; a neutral leaves it red. Blue litmus can't help, since neither is acidic.

q.t: Who is called the Father of Modern Indian Chemistry?
q.e: Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray started India's first pharmaceutical company in 1901 and founded modern chemistry research in India.

q.t: A student says: "Adding a base to an acid always makes the mixture neutral." Why is this not always true?
o: Too much base makes it basic
Acid and base make more acid
q.e: Neutralisation needs the right amounts. Add too little base and it's still acidic; too much and it becomes basic.
